slides.title: Browsing couples visual selection to head placement
body: A giraffe selects leaves with an extensible tongue while positioning its head among branches. Coimbra and colleagues examined the retina, the light-sensitive neural sheet at the back of the eye, to identify spatial specializations associated with browsing and surveillance from an elevated head.

**Retinal ganglion cells** are output neurons whose axons transmit retinal information toward the brain. Their distribution is uneven: the giraffe has a horizontal band of high density, a temporal concentration, and a dorsal arch. Different regions therefore sample different parts of visual space with different spatial precision.

The temporal concentration is associated with frontal visual space, where tongue contact and leaf selection occur. The dorsal arch samples the lower visual field, giving an elevated animal additional spatial resolution toward the ground. These are anatomical interpretations of the retinal organization, rather than measurements of foraging-related neural firing.

slides.title: Brain mass must be interpreted relative to body size
body: The giraffe has a large brain within terrestrial even-toed ungulates. Graïc and colleagues combined their anatomical measurements with independent specimens described in earlier literature. The pooled adult brain mass was approximately 720 g, alongside an average body mass of about 846 kg.

An **encephalization quotient** compares an animal’s brain mass with the mass expected for its body size under a specified mammalian scaling relationship. The authors obtained a quotient of 0.64 for the pooled giraffe data. Absolute brain mass and relative brain size answer different anatomical questions.

The sampled brains had a convoluted cerebral surface, laterally expanded temporal regions, and a well-developed olfactory-associated forebrain. Brain mass therefore provides a scale for the tissue, while surface configuration and neuronal organization identify the structures through which sensory information and motor activity are organized.

slides.title: Cerebral folds provide landmarks for cortical anatomy
body: A **sulcus** is a groove in the cerebral surface, and a **gyrus** is the ridge between grooves. Graïc and colleagues examined preserved giraffe brains and compared surface landmarks with earlier descriptions. Their anatomical comparison used established veterinary nomenclature and bovine brains as additional reference material.

The giraffe cerebrum is extensively folded. Recognizable grooves include the cruciate, coronal, marginal, and ansate sulci. Naming these grooves makes it possible to describe where a cortical sample was taken without assuming that every external fold has a single behavioral function.

The authors compared alternative names previously assigned to the same surface features. Consistent landmarks support comparison across giraffe studies: a motor cortical specimen can be located relative to named sulci, while microscopy identifies the layered tissue and neurons that distinguish it from adjacent cortex.

slides.title: Lateral anatomy includes olfactory and temporal regions
body: The giraffe brain retains the major external organization of terrestrial even-toed ungulates. Graïc and colleagues described a laterally enlarged temporal lobe and an olfactory-associated forebrain visible from the side. The **temporal lobe** is a lateral cerebral region; the **rhinencephalon** refers to forebrain structures associated with olfaction.

The cerebellum lies behind the cerebral hemispheres and is partially covered by them. Its midline region, the **vermis**, is strongly folded and has a distinctive curved surface configuration in the examined giraffe brains. These relationships establish the relative positions of cerebral and cerebellar tissue.

Surface examination supplies the spatial framework for histological sampling. The cortex occupies the folded outer cerebrum, whereas deeper motor pathways pass through internal structures. Gross anatomy and cellular anatomy are therefore complementary descriptions of the same nervous system at different spatial scales.

slides.title: Large eyes contain a regionally organized retina
body: Coimbra and colleagues examined intact giraffe eyes and prepared the retinal tissue for wholemount analysis. The mean eye diameter was about 48 mm along the nasal–temporal axis, and the mean axial length, measured from front to back, was about 42 mm.

A **retinal wholemount** is a flattened preparation of the retinal sheet that preserves the spatial arrangement of its cells. This approach relates local cell density to position within the eye. A cross-section provides depth information, whereas a wholemount retains the broad map of retinal specializations.

The eye’s dimensions enter the anatomical estimate of spatial resolving power because they affect the distance over which an optical image is projected. Cell spacing and optical geometry must be considered together: a densely populated retinal region samples more finely, and the eye’s scale relates that spacing to visual angle.

slides.title: The dorsal tapetum supports photon capture in dim light
body: The **tapetum lucidum** is a reflective tissue behind the retina that returns unabsorbed light through the photoreceptors. A second passage increases the opportunity for photon capture. Coimbra and colleagues observed a greenish-blue tapetum covering the dorsal half of the giraffe eyecup.

A **photoreceptor** is a retinal cell that converts absorbed light into a change in electrical activity. The tapetum acts optically before retinal output is carried by ganglion cells. Its reflective surface differs from the darkly pigmented tissue occupying the remaining choroid, the vascular layer behind the retina.

The dorsal reflective region aligns broadly with retinal specializations directed toward the lower visual field. The authors linked this arrangement to browsing and vigilance in dim conditions. Optical sensitivity and spatial sampling are separate features, yet both are regionally organized within the same giraffe eye.

slides.title: Wholemount sampling preserves the retinal spatial map
body: The giraffe retina was cut radially and flattened so that its curved surface could be examined systematically. Coimbra and colleagues stained the ganglion-cell layer with a Nissl method, which labels cell-body material and helps distinguish neurons from smaller supporting cells.

**Stereology** estimates tissue quantities using systematically sampled observation sites. The researchers adjusted sampling to regions with different cell densities and examined the entire thickness of the ganglion-cell layer at each site. This was especially important where cells formed several sublayers rather than a single plane.

The flattened retina retained temporal, nasal, dorsal, and ventral orientation. Those landmarks connect a microscopic cell count with a part of visual space. The resulting map combined regional counts with their retinal positions instead of treating the entire eye as a uniform sensory surface.

slides.title: Ganglion cells are distinguished from nearby glial cells
body: A retinal wholemount contains both output neurons and non-neuronal supporting cells. Coimbra and colleagues identified ganglion cells by the appearance of their cell bodies, including a pale nucleus, a conspicuous nucleolus, and Nissl-stained cytoplasm. **Glial cells** are supporting cells with different nuclear and cytoplasmic appearances.

The criteria were applied at high magnification across regions with sparse, intermediate, and dense cell packing. Dense packing makes cell boundaries harder to separate, so the preparation was examined through its depth rather than counted from a single focal plane.

These distinctions determine the biological meaning of a density map. A concentration of ganglion cells indicates increased sampling by retinal output neurons; a concentration of all stained nuclei would mix output neurons with supporting cells. Morphological identification therefore links the count specifically to the retina’s information channels.

slides.title: A horizontal visual streak samples the horizon
body: A **visual streak** is an elongated retinal region containing a high density of ganglion cells. In the giraffe it runs approximately horizontally through and above the optic disc, the site where output axons leave the eye, along the nasal–temporal direction.

Coimbra and colleagues mapped density contours across the whole retina. The streak extended beyond the localized temporal concentration and contained much denser cell packing than the dorsal arch. This geometry allocates fine sampling across an extended band rather than concentrating all resolution at one point.

A horizontal retinal specialization is associated with improved sampling along the visual horizon. The giraffe shares this arrangement with several other even-toed ungulates. Its retinal organization combines a broad horizon-related feature with additional specializations associated with the elevated head and frontal browsing space.

slides.title: The temporal area concentrates frontal spatial sampling
body: The **temporal area** is a localized high-density ganglion-cell region on the temporal side of the giraffe retina. Within the temporal arm of the visual streak, density contours became increasingly concentrated around a peak of approximately 14,300 ganglion cells/mm².

At the peak, cells were densely packed in two or three sublayers. Coimbra and colleagues examined different focal depths to count cells throughout this thick region. Dense output sampling reduces the spatial interval between neighboring retinal channels within the corresponding visual field.

The temporal retinal area corresponds to frontal visual space. Leaf selection and tongue contact occur in that space during browsing. The authors interpreted the specialization as supporting fine discrimination of nearby food items, while its position also retains the broader horizon sampling supplied by the horizontal streak.

slides.title: A dorsal arch extends sampling toward the ground
body: The giraffe retina contains a **dorsal arch**, a curved region of elevated ganglion-cell density above the horizontal visual streak. The arch begins with a dorsotemporal extension and tapers toward the nasal side, connecting the two sides of the retinal map.

Densities within the arch were about 250–300 cells/mm². The region immediately above it contained about 40 cells/mm², while the region below contained about 200 cells/mm². The arch is therefore a distinct local increase, although its density is much lower than that of the temporal peak.

Because the optical image is inverted, dorsal retinal tissue samples the lower visual field. The authors related this arrangement to the giraffe’s elevated head, which can be around 5 m above ground. A lower-field specialization complements the visual streak by allocating additional sampling toward nearby terrain.

slides.title: Alpha ganglion cells form a distinct retinal population
body: **Alpha ganglion cells** are large retinal output neurons with distinctive cell bodies and dendritic organization. Coimbra and colleagues used an antibody against neurofilament-200, a neuronal cytoskeletal protein, to identify this population within the giraffe ganglion-cell layer.

The labeled cells were examined in retinal wholemounts so that both their individual morphology and their spatial distribution could be assessed. The labeling also revealed axon bundles associated with ganglion-cell output. This preparation separated the alpha-cell map from the map based on all morphologically identified ganglion cells.

Alpha cells occupied a dorsal arch with stronger concentrations in temporal and dorsonasal regions. The authors associated this cell class with motion information. Their anatomical specialization offers a route for sampling movement in the lower and frontal visual fields during browsing and surveillance.

slides.title: Alpha-cell peaks divide the dorsal arch into regions
body: The alpha ganglion-cell distribution was not a smaller copy of the total ganglion-cell map. Coimbra and colleagues found a dorsal–ventral density gradient and an arch with temporal and dorsonasal peaks. Alpha-cell density reached about 14–15 cells/mm² temporally and about 10 cells/mm² dorsonasally.

The temporal peak lies in a region associated with frontal visual space, while the dorsal distribution emphasizes the lower field. A retinal population can therefore have its own topography even when it occupies the same neural sheet as other ganglion-cell types.

The authors proposed that the temporal specialization contributes motion information during tongue-guided leaf collection, while the dorsonasal concentration assists detection of movement toward the ground. This hypothesis connects the distribution of a particular output-cell class to the spatial demands of feeding and predator surveillance.

slides.title: Cell spacing predicts fine spatial resolving power
body: **Spatial resolving power** is the ability to distinguish closely spaced visual features, expressed here as cycles per degree of visual angle. Coimbra and colleagues estimated it from ganglion-cell spacing in the temporal peak and the optical scale of the giraffe eye.

The anatomical upper estimates were about 25–27 cycles/degree. A cycle consists of one repeated light-and-dark spatial pattern. More closely spaced output cells permit finer sampling, provided that the optical image and upstream retinal processing preserve the corresponding detail.

These values are anatomical estimates rather than behavioral acuity measurements from trained giraffes. The distinction changes how the number should be interpreted. The retinal map nevertheless identifies the temporal area as the region with the greatest potential for fine spatial discrimination within the examined eye.

slides.title: Visual and motor cortex differ in their layered structure
body: The **neocortex** is the layered outer cerebral tissue involved in sensory and motor processing. Jacobs and colleagues examined primary visual and primary motor cortex using Nissl staining for cell bodies and myelin staining for fiber organization. **Myelin** is the insulating material surrounding many axons.

A recognizable layer IV was present in the visual cortex, together with a myelin-rich band in its lower portion, the **stria of Gennari**. Motor cortex lacked a clearly defined layer IV and contained conspicuous large pyramidal neurons in layer V. The regions therefore differed in cellular and fiber architecture.

Layers I and III were relatively thick in both regions. Anatomical identification combined these layered features with the cortical sampling location. Visual and motor tissue share the general cortical plan while organizing its layers differently, providing distinct local environments for the neurons reconstructed in the same study.

slides.title: Pyramidal neurons span cortical depth with apical dendrites
body: A **pyramidal neuron** is a cortical neuron with a prominent dendrite extending from the top of its cell body and additional dendrites emerging below it. **Dendrites** are branching neuronal processes that receive synaptic inputs. Jacobs and colleagues reconstructed these cells after Golgi staining, which reveals individual neurons and their branches.

Typical giraffe pyramidal cells had an apical dendrite extending toward the cortical surface and basilar dendrites radiating around the soma, or cell body. Some apical dendrites reached approximately 1,500 μm in length and extended into superficial cortical layers.

These vertically oriented processes contributed to a columnar organization of dendrites across cortical depth. Superficial pyramidal cells tended to have more divergent apical branches, while deeper cells often had longer, less bifurcating apical dendrites. The arrangement links the position of a neuron with the cortical territory available to its branches.

slides.title: Dendritic spines add input sites to cortical neurons
body: **Dendritic spines** are small protrusions from dendrites that provide sites for many synaptic contacts. Jacobs and colleagues measured the branches and spines of individually stained giraffe cortical neurons. A **synapse** is a specialized contact through which one neuron influences another.

Typical pyramidal cells were spiny, while other neurons had different combinations of dendritic orientation, branch extent, and spine density. The study distinguished ordinary pyramidal cells, larger pyramidal forms, horizontally oriented cells, and superficially branching extraverted cells within this morphological diversity.

Typical pyramidal neurons in motor cortex had greater spine density than those in visual cortex, even though their overall dendritic complexity was similar. The regional difference therefore involved the density of potential input sites along dendrites, rather than a simple replacement of the general pyramidal branching plan.

slides.title: Motor cortex contains large spiny projection neurons
body: **Gigantopyramidal neurons** are unusually large pyramidal cells identified in giraffe motor cortex. Jacobs and colleagues found them deeper in the cortex, around 1,500 μm below the surface, with large cell bodies, an ascending apical dendrite, and numerous basilar branches.

Their basilar dendrites formed a dense arrangement around the soma. These cells had a more extensive dendritic system than ordinary pyramidal neurons and the highest density of basilar branch intersections among the spiny cell types examined. Their dendrites also carried abundant spines.

The combination of a large soma, multiple basilar branches, and an ascending apical dendrite establishes a broad anatomical territory for incoming contacts. Badlangana and colleagues identified clustered large layer V cells in motor cortex as the likely origin of descending corticospinal fibers, connecting this cortical cell population with spinal motor organization.

slides.title: Local-circuit neurons vary in branching orientation
body: **Local-circuit neurons** organize activity within a nearby neural region rather than sending their main output to a distant target. Jacobs and colleagues reconstructed aspiny neurons, whose dendrites lacked the conspicuous spines of pyramidal cells, throughout giraffe visual and motor cortex.

Some cells had multipolar dendrites radiating in several directions; others had elongated or vertically oriented branching patterns. Their dendritic density and branch length varied substantially. The reconstructions therefore revealed a local-cell population with several anatomical forms, distributed across cortical depth.

The morphology of these cells resembled forms reported in other placental mammals. The giraffe cortex combines specialized regional features, such as the prominent motor projection neurons, with local-circuit architectures shared across species. Cortical organization includes both long-range output cells and neighboring cells with different input territories.

slides.title: Newborn cortex already contains recognizable cell classes
body: Jacobs and colleagues examined newborn giraffe cortex to ask how neuronal organization compares with later development. They used a modified Golgi preparation and computer-assisted reconstructions to quantify dendritic branching and spine distributions. **Ontogeny** is the development of an individual organism.

The newborn giraffe already contained recognizable pyramidal, extraverted, gigantopyramidal, and local-circuit neuron forms. An extraverted neuron has branches that divide near the soma and extend prominently toward superficial tissue. Distinct neuronal architectures were therefore present at birth.

Newborn projection neurons were smaller than corresponding adult forms, even when their overall shape was recognizable. **Projection neurons** send axonal output beyond the immediate local circuit. Their continued dendritic growth expands the cortical territory available for inputs while preserving many features of their original cell-class organization.

slides.title: Projection-neuron dendrites expand after birth
body: The newborn-to-adult comparison separated neuronal form from neuronal size. Jacobs and colleagues found recognizable pyramidal and extraverted shapes in newborn giraffe cortex, but their dendritic systems were smaller than those of corresponding adult cells from earlier measurements.

The comparison considered dendritic length, branch organization, soma size, and spine measures. An adult neuron can retain the same general orientation while increasing its total dendritic extent. Growth therefore changes the amount of neural tissue available for synaptic input without necessarily creating a new morphological cell class.

Local-circuit neurons followed a different pattern: their newborn and adult sizes were approximately similar in the comparison. Development was consequently selective across cell classes. Long-range projection cells underwent substantial expansion, while much of the local-cell dendritic scaffold was already established in newborn cortex.

slides.title: Transient spines distinguish newborn local neurons
body: Newborn giraffe local-circuit neurons included multipolar, bipolar, and neurogliaform forms. A **bipolar neuron** has two dominant opposing dendritic directions, while a **neurogliaform neuron** has relatively compact, densely branching processes. Jacobs and colleagues identified these forms by their cell-body and dendritic architecture.

Many newborn local neurons carried dendritic spines, in contrast to the generally aspiny adult forms used for comparison. A cell class can therefore change the surface organization of its input branches even when its overall dendritic size remains approximately similar.

The authors discussed these early spines as a developmental feature of local neuronal organization. The transition from spiny newborn branches to more aspiny adult branches differs from the marked dendritic growth of projection neurons. Cortical maturation involves changes in both branch extent and the fine structure of individual dendrites.

slides.title: Elephant and giraffe neurons differ from birth
body: Jacobs and colleagues compared newborn giraffe and African elephant cortex using the same staining and reconstruction approach. Both species contained recognizable projection neurons and local-circuit cells, but the elephant neurons had more extensive dendritic systems across the principal measures examined.

Elephant projection neurons also included a broader variety of morphologies, such as flattened pyramidal and nonpyramidal multipolar cells. A **nonpyramidal multipolar cell** has several major dendritic directions without the conventional single ascending apical organization of a typical pyramidal neuron.

Species differences were therefore present at birth rather than arising only through adult experience. Giraffe projection cells retained a comparatively conventional pyramidal organization, whereas the elephant exhibited additional forms and larger arbors. This comparison places giraffe development within the diversity of large mammalian cortical architecture.

slides.title: Motor layer V contains clusters of large pyramidal cells
body: Badlangana and colleagues used Nissl-stained sections to identify the cellular organization of giraffe primary motor cortex. **Primary motor cortex**, or M1, is a cortical region associated with descending control of voluntary movement. Its layer V contained conspicuous clusters of large pyramidal cells.

The clustered cells had soma areas of approximately 600 μm², with their apical dendrites often converging into a small bundle. A **fasciculus** is a bundle of nerve processes. The cells were distributed across layer V in small groups rather than as isolated giant neurons.

This architecture resembled the motor cortex described in sheep. The finding contrasts with the prediction that the giraffe’s long neck requires exceptionally enlarged, primate-like motor cells. At the examined anatomical scale, the giraffe retained an ungulate-like cellular arrangement alongside its unusually elongated body.

slides.title: The cervical cord accounts for much of spinal length
body: The **spinal cord** contains neural tissue connecting the brain with segmentally organized sensory and motor circuits. Badlangana and colleagues exposed and measured the giraffe cord along the vertebral column. The longest measured cord was 2.6 m, extending to the sacral vertebrae.

The cervical portion, associated with the neck, measured 1.4 m in that specimen and accounted for much of the total length. The **conus medullaris**, the tapered end of the spinal cord, was located near the sacrum, a pattern also found in other ungulates.

Sections taken at cervical, thoracic, and lumbar levels retained a recognizable mammalian organization. The long cervical cord therefore extends an existing segmental plan across a greater distance. Its length changes the spatial scale of neural communication, while its local gray- and white-matter organization remains comparable with that of other mammals.

slides.title: The internal capsule channels descending cortical fibers
body: The **internal capsule** is a concentrated pathway of axons passing through deep cerebral tissue. Badlangana and colleagues compared cell-body and myelin-stained giraffe sections to identify this pathway in relation to the caudate nucleus and putamen, two components of the dorsal striatum.

The internal capsule divided the deep striatopallidal complex into recognizable regions. The **globus pallidus** is a pallidal region adjacent to the striatum. Fibers associated with descending cortical output coalesced within this anatomically recognizable route through the brain.

The pathway continued toward the cerebral peduncles, fiber bundles at the base of the midbrain, and then toward the pons. The proposed corticospinal route in the giraffe thus follows the familiar mammalian sequence of deep cerebral and brainstem structures between cortical motor neurons and spinal circuitry.

slides.title: Medullary pyramids carry the descending pathway
body: The **medulla oblongata** is the brainstem region immediately above the spinal cord. Myelin-stained giraffe sections revealed paired pyramidal tracts along its ventral midline. A **tract** is a bundle of axons following a shared route through the central nervous system.

The pyramids were broad from side to side and flattened in the dorsal–ventral direction. They lay below the inferior olives, recognizable brainstem nuclei. Their anatomical position matched the descending route described in other mammals, connecting the cerebral pathway with the spinal cord.

The pyramidal crossing, or **decussation**, occurred about 2 mm before the beginning of the cervical cord. Crossing changes the side on which descending fibers travel. The authors reconstructed the likely corticospinal route from these anatomical landmarks; its complete spinal termination would require tract-tracing evidence.

slides.title: Spinal gray matter increases toward the lumbar region
body: **Gray matter** contains neuronal cell bodies and local processes, while **white matter** is dominated by axonal pathways. Badlangana and colleagues compared giraffe spinal sections stained for cell bodies and myelin at cervical, thoracic, and lumbar levels.

The lumbar region contained more gray matter in both absolute and relative terms than the cervical region. The dorsal horn, intermediate region, and ventral horn remained readily identifiable at the examined levels. A **horn** is an anatomically defined extension of spinal gray matter in cross-section.

Regional proportions therefore changed along the cord without replacing its overall organization. Sensory-associated dorsal tissue, motor-associated ventral tissue, and surrounding axonal routes occupied corresponding positions. The long giraffe cord combines continuity of its basic plan with regional differences in the amount of tissue devoted to local circuits.

slides.title: Ventral-horn neurons retain cholinergic organization
body: **Acetylcholine** is a neurotransmitter, a chemical released by neurons to influence their targets. The **vesicular acetylcholine transporter**, or VAChT, loads acetylcholine into synaptic vesicles before release. Badlangana and colleagues used transporter immunolabeling to identify cholinergic organization in giraffe spinal tissue.

Large labeled motor neurons were present in the ventral horn at cervical, thoracic, and lumbar levels. A **motor neuron** sends output toward muscle, and the ventral horn contains the spinal cell bodies associated with that output. Labeled terminals also surrounded these neuronal populations.

The arrangement matched the cholinergic spinal organization described in other mammals. The labeling identifies the anatomical machinery for packaging a transmitter within a motor-associated region. These tissue measurements establish transmitter-related organization rather than measuring acetylcholine release or receptor responses during an actual neck movement.

slides.title: Dorsal spinal laminae also contain cholinergic terminals
body: The **dorsal horn** is the sensory-associated portion of spinal gray matter. It is subdivided into laminae, layers distinguished by cellular and connectional organization. Badlangana and colleagues observed strong vesicular acetylcholine transporter labeling in giraffe dorsal laminae II and especially III.

This distribution occurred at cervical, thoracic, and lumbar levels. The labeled terminal fields differed from the large cholinergic cell bodies of the ventral horn. **Axon terminals** are the ends of axonal branches where signals can be transmitted to other cells.

The authors proposed that much of the dorsal cholinergic innervation belongs to local interneurons, as described in other mammals. The same transmitter-associated machinery is therefore present in anatomically different circuit components: local sensory-associated processing regions and motor-associated output neurons, each with its own spatial organization.

slides.title: CGRP labeling emphasizes superficial sensory regions
body: **Calcitonin gene-related peptide**, or CGRP, is a signaling peptide associated with populations of sensory neurons. Badlangana and colleagues used an antibody against CGRP to examine the giraffe spinal cord. **Immunohistochemistry** locates a molecular target in tissue using antibody-based labeling.

Strong terminal labeling occupied the marginal layer, or lamina I, and part of the substantia gelatinosa, a superficial dorsal-horn region corresponding to lamina II. The same broad distribution occurred in cervical, thoracic, and lumbar sections, while labeling in deeper regions was sparser.

The authors connected this pattern with primary sensory terminal distributions previously described in other mammals. A **primary sensory neuron** carries information from peripheral tissue into the nervous system. The giraffe dorsal horn thus retains a peptide-associated sensory arrangement across the large distances imposed by its elongated neck and spinal cord.

slides.title: Superficial neck muscles span the elongated skeleton
body: Endo and colleagues dissected the giraffe neck to document the positions and attachments of muscles associated with head support and movement. The **splenius capitis** and **splenius cervicis** occupied a superficial layer along the dorsal and lateral neck, just beneath the skin.

These muscles were thin and long, following a relatively direct course from the thoracic region toward the occipital part of the skull. **Occipital** refers to the rear of the skull. Their geometry followed the elongated skeletal framework rather than forming short isolated units around a single cervical joint.

The dissection distinguished superficial muscles from deeper systems revealed after the splenius layer was reflected. Head and neck support is therefore distributed across several anatomical levels. Long superficial muscles coexist with deeper muscles and tendons attached to individual vertebral processes, linking broad neck orientation with more localized skeletal attachments.

These muscles were thin and long, following a relatively direct course from the thoracic region toward the occipital part of the skull. Occipital refers to the rear of the skull. Their geometry followed the elongated skeletal framework rather than forming short isolated units around a single cervical joint.

The dissection distinguished superficial muscles from deeper systems revealed after the splenius layer was reflected. Head and neck support is therefore distributed across several anatomical levels. Long superficial muscles coexist with deeper muscles and tendons attached to individual vertebral processes, linking broad neck orientation with more localized skeletal attachments.

slides.title: Longissimus combines long bellies with strong tendons
body: The **longissimus** is a longitudinal muscle system lying deeper than the splenius in the giraffe neck. Endo and colleagues described cervical longissimus muscles with two parallel bellies and strong tendons extending to the transverse processes of cervical vertebrae.

A **muscle belly** is the contractile portion of a muscle, while a **tendon** connects that tissue with its attachment. A **transverse process** is a lateral projection of a vertebra. The cervical muscles ran from caudal vertebral regions toward more cranial attachments along the neck.

The elongated bellies and tendons occupied the spaces associated with the giraffe’s long vertebrae. Broad attachment areas on the modified bony processes provided a structural connection between muscle force and skeletal movement. The anatomy distributes support and movement-related attachments over the full length of the neck.

slides.title: Cranial tendons connect neck muscles to the head
body: Near the skull, Endo and colleagues identified longissimus atlantis and longissimus capitis muscles with long tendons. **Capitis** indicates a head-related attachment, while **atlantis** refers to the atlas, the first cervical vertebra supporting the skull.

The longissimus atlantis tendon extended toward the transverse process of the atlas, and the longissimus capitis system extended toward the occipital bone. Other tendons attached near the axis, the second cervical vertebra. These attachment differences connect related muscle systems with different skeletal targets.

A median fibrous raphe, a connective-tissue seam along the dorsal midline, contributed another origin for part of the muscle system. The cranial neck therefore includes attachments to vertebrae, skull, and connective tissue. Their spatial arrangement transfers the action of elongated muscles to structures that position the head.

slides.title: Deep extensor muscles occupy expanded vertebral spaces
body: Endo and colleagues described a deep muscular complex containing thoracic and cervical spinalis and semispinalis components. These muscles lay beneath the longissimus and had elongated bellies enlarged in the dorsal–ventral direction along the lateral surfaces of the cervical vertebrae.

Fibers extended from the spinous processes and medial transverse regions of caudal vertebrae toward more cranial spinous processes. A **spinous process** is a dorsal projection of a vertebra. These bony projections provided the attachment surfaces through which the deep muscle complex acted on the skeleton.

Between the third and fifth cervical vertebrae, the muscle complex attached along and covered the nuchal ligament. Its anatomy therefore joined active contractile tissue with a passive supporting structure. The enlarged bellies occupied long intervertebral spaces while the broad attachments connected the complex with the elongated neck framework.

slides.title: The nuchal ligament provides passive neck support
body: The **nuchal ligament** is a strong fibrous structure along the dorsal neck that contributes passive support. Endo and colleagues exposed it by reflecting the deeper extensor complex. It was well developed and connected with the spinous region of the axis and the dorsal head-muscle system.

The ligament covered the spinous process of the atlas and was associated with muscles along the neck. Beneath it, multifidus muscle bellies extended along the vertebral bodies. One described belly was about 350 mm long, reflecting the scale of the giraffe’s cervical skeleton.

The authors interpreted the broad ligament and muscle attachments as supporting the heavy head and long neck. Passive tissue support and active muscle action are anatomically interlinked: the ligament contributes a supporting structure, while associated muscle bellies and tendons provide the capacity to alter position and maintain orientation.

slides.title: Atlas and axis specialize the cranial neck framework
body: The **atlas** is the first cervical vertebra, and the **axis** is the second. Endo and colleagues examined their shapes and measured the cranial cervical skeleton. The atlas had expanded wings and broad articular surfaces, while the axis had an elongated body and enlarged attachment processes.

An **articular surface** is the bony surface participating in a joint. The atlas measured about 156 mm in greatest length in the measured specimen. The axis body measured 261 mm, emphasizing that neighboring cranial vertebrae differ substantially in shape as well as size.

The wings and processes receive tendons and muscles described in the same dissection. The head-supporting end of the neck therefore combines joint surfaces with extensive attachment areas. These anatomical features connect the elongated muscle systems with the skeletal elements immediately beneath the skull.

slides.title: Short cranial muscles link adjacent neck structures
body: Endo and colleagues identified dorsal, intermediate, and ventral cervical **intertransversarius muscles**, which occupy positions between transverse regions of adjacent cervical structures. The dorsal component was larger than the other two, and the three components were anatomically distinguishable.

Near the atlas, the cranial oblique muscle of the head arose from its transverse process. The semispinalis capitis included biventer cervicis and complexus components, continuous with the more caudal deep muscle complex. These names identify particular parts of the cranial neck’s layered muscle arrangement.

The dissected anatomy combines long muscle systems spanning much of the neck with more localized attachments near neighboring vertebrae and the skull. Broad head orientation and the mechanics of the cranial joints therefore depend on multiple overlapping structures rather than one long muscle acting alone.

slides.title: Neutral neck curvature emerges from joint geometry
body: Vidal and colleagues reconstructed articulated giraffe skeletons to examine the motion permitted by their bones. An **osteologically neutral pose** aligns neighboring vertebrae with their articular facets in full overlap. **Osteological** means that the estimate is based on bony anatomy.

In the adult giraffe reconstruction, the atlas lay at a 26° angle relative to the first thoracic vertebra in this neutral arrangement. Most of the upward deflection occurred near the junction between the thorax and the caudal cervical vertebrae, where the vertebral bodies were wedge-shaped.

The more cranial cervical bodies articulated approximately straight, contributing only a small additional deflection. An elevated neck posture therefore arises partly from the shape and alignment of particular joints. Active muscles operate within a skeletal framework whose neutral curvature is already unevenly distributed along the neck.

slides.title: Adult neck motion spans a large vertical range
body: Vidal and colleagues rotated the articulated cervical bones while retaining joint contact to estimate adult giraffe range of motion. **Dorsiflexion** bends the neck upward, while **ventriflexion** bends it downward. These measurements describe motion permitted by the reconstructed skeleton.

The atlas could reach about 103° relative to the first thoracic vertebra in maximum dorsiflexion and about −73° in maximum ventriflexion. The reconstruction placed the muzzle as high as 4.1 m, but neck flexion alone left it about 0.45 m above ground at its lowest position.

Reaching ground level therefore requires changes beyond bending the neck alone, such as altering the position of the limbs and body. The skeletal estimate links a range of cervical joint motion with the whole-body geometry needed for drinking or accessing low vegetation.

slides.title: Lateral flexion redistributes overlap between joint facets
body: The giraffe’s cervical joints contain paired **zygapophyses**, bony articular processes that overlap between neighboring vertebrae. Vidal and colleagues examined lateral flexion by changing the overlap on the two sides while retaining contact, rather than applying a single fixed overlap threshold to every posture.

In the adult reconstruction, the neck could curve through more than 180° in the horizontal plane, allowing the head to reach the body before the joints disarticulated. **Disarticulation** is the loss of normal joint contact. The permitted posture depended on how the paired facets moved relative to one another.

The authors compared the reconstructed postures with observations of living giraffes and found that extreme neck positions could retain articulation. A large lateral movement is therefore compatible with continuing joint contact. Neck flexibility reflects coordinated changes across multiple joints rather than a single unusually mobile vertebra.

slides.title: Newborn vertebral spacing differs from adult spacing
body: Vidal and colleagues examined a newborn giraffe with computed tomography, or **CT**, which reconstructs internal anatomy from X-ray measurements. The scan preserved the positions of bones before the individual vertebrae were separated digitally for articulation tests.

The newborn cervical skeleton had substantial intervertebral spaces, the gaps between adjacent vertebral bodies. In the neutral reconstruction these spaces accounted for about 27% of the examined neck segment, compared with about 4.8% in the adult. Some cervical regions were also incompletely or asymmetrically ossified.

**Ossification** is the formation of bone tissue. Growth changes the relation between mineralized vertebrae and the spaces occupied by intervening tissue. The adult skeleton is therefore an inadequate template for the newborn neck unless these developmental differences in shape and joint spacing are included.

slides.title: Growth alters joint spacing and neck mobility
body: The reconstructed newborn and adult necks differed in both posture and mobility. Vidal and colleagues found that the newborn neutral neck formed a steeper angle, about 39° between the first thoracic vertebra and atlas, than the adult neutral neck’s 26°.

The newborn reconstruction reached about 91° in maximum dorsiflexion and about −46° in ventriflexion. Its estimated muzzle-height range was approximately 0.49–1.47 m. The adult had a greater overall bony range of motion despite possessing proportionally smaller intervertebral spaces.

Development therefore changes more than the length of the neck. Vertebral shape, neutral curvature, joint spacing, and permitted rotation change together. The relationship between spacing and flexibility cannot be inferred from gap size alone, because the shapes and orientations of the articular surfaces also determine the movements available to the growing animal.

slides.title: Sensory and motor anatomy changes at different scales
body: Giraffe head placement depends on an elongated mechanical system and anatomically organized neural pathways. Endo and colleagues documented long muscle bellies, tendons, and ligament attachments, while Badlangana and colleagues identified a motor cortex and descending pathway retaining an ungulate-like anatomical arrangement.

The retina allocates fine spatial sampling to the frontal field and additional sampling toward the ground. Cortical neurons organize inputs across dendritic trees, and large motor-layer cells are associated anatomically with the descending corticospinal route. These studies connect sensory tissue, cortical organization, and the structures operating the neck.

Development changes both sides of this relationship: projection-neuron dendrites expand after birth, while cervical joint geometry and bony mobility also change. A long neck is therefore supported by coordinated changes in several tissues, with specialized sensory and mechanical features coexisting with broadly conserved mammalian neural organization.
